Your perception surprises you

The Ebbinghaus circles

A circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller than an identical one surrounded by small ones.

The illusion is named after Hermann Ebbinghaus, known for his studies of memory, although Edward Titchener popularised it in the early twentieth century. Two identical circles look different sizes depending on the circles around them.

Size is relative

The visual system does not measure objects in isolation but in comparison with their surroundings. A 1995 study found something curious: although the eye is fooled, when people reached to pick up a disc, the opening of their fingers matched its real size closely. It was proposed that vision for recognising and vision for acting work partly separately, though later studies have qualified this result.

There are also cultural differences: some rural communities in Namibia, such as the Himba, are less susceptible to this illusion than people living in Western cities.

References

  1. Aglioti, S., DeSouza, J. F. y Goodale, M. A. (1995). Size-contrast illusions deceive the eye but not the hand. Current Biology, 5(6), 679–685.
  2. de Fockert, J., Davidoff, J., Fagot, J., Parron, C. y Goldstein, J. (2007). More accurate size contrast judgments in the Ebbinghaus illusion by a remote culture. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 33(3), 738–742.
